meta: A leaderboard tells you which model is best, but not whether your product is good. Three ways AI product makers measure: sample questions from real customers, signals from real users, and A/B tests.

muc.title: Leaderboards aren't enough
muc.text: A leaderboard says this model is the best. But whether your product is good, a leaderboard can't tell you.

muc.title: A set of sample questions
muc.text: The first way: a set of sample questions, taken from real customer questions, with the right answers. A bakery might have fifty: cake prices, opening hours, how to order.

muc.title: Rerun it every time you change something
muc.text: Every time you change something, the model or the instructions, rerun the whole set. Any question that used to be right and is now wrong shows up right away, before customers see it.

muc.title: Signals from real users
muc.text: The second way: listen to real users. Not just the like and dislike buttons. If they ask the same thing again, they weren't satisfied. If they edit the answer before using it, it was close. If they leave halfway, something's wrong.

muc.title: A/B testing
muc.text: The third way: an A/B test. Half the customers see the old version, half see the new one. Whichever gets more cake orders wins.

muc.title: Three ways together
muc.text: All three together: the question set keeps quality steady, real signals show where it hurts, and A/B tests help you choose a direction.

muc.title: Click the button, add a reason
muc.text: Next time you see like and dislike buttons in an AI app, click one, and add a line saying why. That's how you help improve the product.

muc.title: Every answer costs money
muc.text: But every answer being measured costs money. How much, and who pays? See you in part 5.
